## Using this document

Open this QMD in RStudio. Run a numbered demonstration with its chunk's
green arrow. **Every numbered chunk is independent:** it defines its own
inputs, functions, and seed. You can jump between sections without running
an earlier chunk. The code uses base R. Rendering uses knitr and rmarkdown.

The HTML shows saved output; edit and run the QMD for live demonstrations.
All examples are hypothetical. The bargaining population and forecast
parameters differ from B2. No student data or homework solutions appear here.

The integral notation in class means accumulating probability over an
interval. These demonstrations use geometry, CDFs, or simulation to do the
calculations. **No hand integration is needed.**

## 1. Waiting times and rectangle areas

Model the waiting time until an outreach worker arrives as
$T\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,10)$ minutes. This is a deliberately simple model,
not an empirical claim about arrival times.

**Predict:** What fraction of waits fall between 2 and 5 minutes?

```{r}
#| label: demo-1-uniform
set.seed(93001)
n_sim <- 50000
waits <- runif(n_sim, min = 0, max = 10)
exact_interval <- punif(5, 0, 10) - punif(2, 0, 10)
data.frame(quantity = c("P(2 <= T <= 5)", "E[T]", "Var(T)"),
           exact = c(exact_interval, 5, 100 / 12),
           simulated = c(mean(waits >= 2 & waits <= 5),
                         mean(waits), var(waits)))
curve(dunif(x, 0, 10), from = -1, to = 11,
      ylim = c(0, .13), col = "#176B87", lwd = 3,
      xlab = "Waiting time (minutes)", ylab = "Density (per minute)")
rect(2, 0, 5, .1, col = "#CEE3EB", border = NA)
segments(0, .1, 10, .1, col = "#176B87", lwd = 3)
epsilon <- c(.5, .1, .01)
center <- 5
narrow_intervals <- data.frame(
  lower = center - epsilon,
  upper = center + epsilon,
  width = 2 * epsilon,
  probability = punif(center + epsilon, 0, 10) -
                punif(center - epsilon, 0, 10)
)
narrow_intervals$probability_per_minute <-
  narrow_intervals$probability / narrow_intervals$width
narrow_intervals
c(density_at_five = dunif(5, 0, 10),
  probability_at_or_below_five = punif(5, 0, 10))
```

The rectangle has width 3 minutes and height 0.1 per minute: area 0.3.
`&` applies both inequalities to every draw. `&&` is not the vector
operation we need here. Change `n_sim` to 500: the probability model and
its variance stay fixed, but the simulation becomes less precise.

In the shrinking-interval table, probabilities approach zero while
probability divided by width remains 0.1 per minute. That local rate is
`dunif(5, 0, 10)`. It does not mean $P(T=5)=0.1$.
`punif(5, 0, 10)` returns a probability for the implicit interval
$(-\infty,5]$, which here is the same event as $0\le T\le5$.

For a density continuous at $x$, this generalizes to

$$f_X(x)=\lim_{\epsilon\downarrow0}
\frac{P(x-\epsilon\le X\le x+\epsilon)}{2\epsilon}.$$

Some authors call a density $p(x)$ instead of $f_X(x)$. Check what the
function represents, rather than assuming its letter means point probability.

## 2. Optional: a sloping density without antiderivatives

Suppose a different waiting-time model has density $f(t)=t/50$ on $[0,10]$.
The whole triangle has area one. Its CDF within the support is
$F(t)=t^2/100$, the area of a triangle of base $t$ and height $t/50$.

The supplied sampling transformation $T=10\sqrt U$, for
$U\sim\operatorname{Unif}(0,1)$, has that CDF. Understanding the density and
CDF is the main task; deriving this sampling method is optional.

```{r}
#| label: demo-2-triangle
set.seed(93002)
n_sim <- 50000
waits <- 10 * sqrt(runif(n_sim))
exact_interval <- (5^2 - 2^2) / 100
trapezoid_area <- (5 - 2) * ((2 / 50) + (5 / 50)) / 2
data.frame(method = c("CDF difference", "Trapezoid area", "Simulation"),
           probability = c(exact_interval, trapezoid_area,
                           mean(waits >= 2 & waits <= 5)))
curve(x / 50, from = 0, to = 10, lwd = 3, col = "#176B87",
      xlab = "Waiting time (minutes)", ylab = "Density (per minute)")
polygon(c(2, 2, 5, 5), c(0, 2 / 50, 5 / 50, 0),
        col = "#CEE3EB", border = NA)
curve(x / 50, add = TRUE, lwd = 3, col = "#176B87")
```

**Ask:** Why is an interval near 8 more likely than an equally wide interval
near 2 under this model? Contrast that with the uniform model.

## 3. Normal density, cumulative probability, and a near-tie

Use the hypothetical forecast $V\sim\operatorname{Norm}(3,5)$, with margin
measured in percentage points and **standard deviation** 5.

**Predict:** Should the win probability exceed one half? Does a density at
zero directly answer a probability question?

```{r}
#| label: demo-3-normal
mu <- 3
sigma <- 5
density_at_zero <- dnorm(0, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
p_win <- pnorm(0, mean = mu, sd = sigma, lower.tail = FALSE)
p_near <- pnorm(1, mu, sigma) - pnorm(-1, mu, sigma)
p_at_or_below_zero <- pnorm(0, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
data.frame(quantity = c("Density at zero (per pp)", "P(V > 0)",
                         "P(-1 <= V <= 1)"),
           value = c(density_at_zero, p_win, p_near))

epsilon <- c(.5, .1, .01)
near_tie <- data.frame(
  epsilon = epsilon,
  exact = pnorm(epsilon, mu, sigma) - pnorm(-epsilon, mu, sigma),
  rectangle = 2 * epsilon * density_at_zero
)
near_tie$probability_per_unit_width <- near_tie$exact / (2 * epsilon)
near_tie

x <- seq(mu - 4 * sigma, mu + 4 * sigma, length.out = 801)
plot(x, dnorm(x, mu, sigma), type = "l", col = "#176B87", lwd = 3,
     xlab = "Vote margin (percentage points)", ylab = "Density (per pp)")
z <- seq(0, max(x), length.out = 401)
polygon(c(0, z, max(z)), c(0, dnorm(z, mu, sigma), 0),
        col = "#CEE3EB", border = NA)
lines(x, dnorm(x, mu, sigma), col = "#176B87", lwd = 3)
abline(v = 0, lty = 2)

# The same lower-tail probability as PDF area and CDF height.
old_par <- par(no.readonly = TRUE)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4.1, 4.1, 2.1, .7))
plot(x, dnorm(x, mu, sigma), type = "l", col = "#176B87", lwd = 3,
     xlab = "Margin (pp)", ylab = "Density (per pp)", main = "Normal PDF")
z <- seq(min(x), 0, length.out = 401)
polygon(c(min(z), z, 0), c(0, dnorm(z, mu, sigma), 0),
        col = "#CEE3EB", border = NA)
lines(x, dnorm(x, mu, sigma), col = "#176B87", lwd = 3)
segments(0, 0, 0, dnorm(0, mu, sigma), lty = 2, col = "#A44A3F")
text(mu - 2.4 * sigma, dnorm(mu, mu, sigma) * .9,
     sprintf("Area = %.3f", p_at_or_below_zero), col = "#A44A3F")
plot(x, pnorm(x, mu, sigma), type = "l", col = "#176B87", lwd = 3,
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Threshold x (pp)",
     ylab = "Cumulative probability", main = "Normal CDF")
segments(min(x), p_at_or_below_zero, 0, p_at_or_below_zero,
         lty = 2, col = "#A44A3F")
segments(0, 0, 0, p_at_or_below_zero, lty = 2, col = "#A44A3F")
points(0, p_at_or_below_zero, pch = 16, col = "#A44A3F")
text(0, p_at_or_below_zero, sprintf("F(0) = %.3f", p_at_or_below_zero),
     pos = 4, col = "#A44A3F", cex = .9)
par(old_par)

# Now vary the mean, keeping SD and the victory threshold fixed.
mean_grid <- seq(-15, 15, length.out = 601)
win_probability <- pnorm(0, mean = mean_grid, sd = sigma, lower.tail = FALSE)
selected_means <- c(-5, 0, 5)
selected_probabilities <- pnorm(selected_means / sigma)
data.frame(assumed_mean = selected_means,
           probability_of_victory = selected_probabilities)
plot(mean_grid, win_probability, type = "l", col = "#176B87", lwd = 3,
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Assumed mean margin (pp)",
     ylab = "Probability of victory")
segments(selected_means, 0, selected_means, selected_probabilities,
         lty = 3, col = "#A44A3F")
points(selected_means, selected_probabilities, pch = 16, col = "#A44A3F")
text(selected_means[1:2], selected_probabilities[1:2],
     sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * selected_probabilities[1:2]),
     pos = c(3, 2), col = "#A44A3F")
text(selected_means[3] + .4, selected_probabilities[3] - .13,
     sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * selected_probabilities[3]),
     pos = 4, col = "#A44A3F")
legend("topleft", sprintf("SD = %g pp; victory requires V > 0", sigma), bty = "n")
```

The near-tie probability tends to zero as the interval shrinks.
Probability **divided by interval width** approaches the density.
The normal curve extends beyond the plot; `pnorm()` includes its full tails.

On the CDF, the horizontal axis moves the **threshold** within the fixed
$\operatorname{Norm}(3,5)$ distribution. On the final graph it changes the
**assumed mean**, holding the victory threshold at zero. With SD 5, means
$-5,0,5$ give victory probabilities of about 16%, 50%, and 84%.

The same increase in mean has a larger probability effect around an even
contest than far out in either tail.

**Try:** Change only `sigma` to 10. Before running, predict the effect on the
chance of a win when the mean remains positive.

## 4. Quantiles and simulation

A central 80% forecast interval leaves 10% in each tail. This interval
describes the random margin under a given model. It is not a confidence
interval for an unknown mean.

```{r}
#| label: demo-4-quantiles
set.seed(93004)
n_sim <- 50000
mu <- 3
sigma <- 5
interval <- qnorm(c(.10, .90), mean = mu, sd = sigma)
margins <- rnorm(n_sim, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
data.frame(quantile = c(.10, .90), margin = interval,
           cdf_check = pnorm(interval, mu, sigma))
comparison <- data.frame(
  quantity = c("P(V > 0)", "P(-1 <= V <= 1)", "Mean", "Variance",
               "Inside central 80%"),
  exact = c(pnorm(0, mu, sigma, lower.tail = FALSE),
            pnorm(1, mu, sigma) - pnorm(-1, mu, sigma),
            mu, sigma^2, .8),
  simulated = c(mean(margins > 0), mean(margins >= -1 & margins <= 1),
                mean(margins), var(margins),
                mean(margins >= interval[1] & margins <= interval[2]))
)
comparison$absolute_difference <- abs(comparison$simulated - comparison$exact)
comparison
x <- seq(mu - 4 * sigma, mu + 4 * sigma, length.out = 801)
probabilities <- c(.10, .90)
plot(x, pnorm(x, mu, sigma), type = "l", col = "#176B87", lwd = 3,
     ylim = c(0, 1), xlab = "Margin threshold (pp)",
     ylab = "Cumulative probability", yaxt = "n")
axis(2, at = c(.1, .5, .9), las = 1)
segments(min(x), probabilities, interval, probabilities,
         lty = 2, col = "#A44A3F")
segments(interval, 0, interval, probabilities, lty = 2, col = "#A44A3F")
points(interval, probabilities, pch = 16, col = "#A44A3F")
text(interval, c(.28, .68), sprintf("%.2f pp", interval),
     pos = c(2, 4), col = "#A44A3F")

hist(margins, probability = TRUE, breaks = 50, col = "#CEE3EB",
     border = "white", main = "Simulated margins and model density",
     xlab = "Vote margin (percentage points)")
curve(dnorm(x, mu, sigma), add = TRUE, lwd = 3, col = "#176B87")
abline(v = interval, lty = 2, col = "#A44A3F")
```

Read the CDF guides from probabilities .10 and .90 across to the curve,
then down to the thresholds. `pnorm(interval, mu, sigma)` checks that
`qnorm()` returned the requested thresholds.

`probability = TRUE` puts histogram **area** on the probability scale.
More repetitions improve Monte Carlo precision. They do not make the
forecast distribution narrower.

## 5. A discrete election and its normal approximation

Suppose exactly 200 people vote for A or B, independently, with probability
0.5 for A. Let $K$ count A's votes. These are explicit toy-model assumptions.

**Predict:** Is an exact tie impossible? Does a strict victory have probability
exactly one half when a tie has positive probability?

```{r}
#| label: demo-5-votes
set.seed(93005)
n_sim <- 50000
n_voters <- 200
p <- .5
mu_count <- n_voters * p
sd_count <- sqrt(n_voters * p * (1 - p))
tie_count <- n_voters / 2
counts <- rbinom(n_sim, size = n_voters, prob = p)

tie_exact <- dbinom(tie_count, n_voters, p)
tie_normal <- pnorm(tie_count + .5, mu_count, sd_count) -
              pnorm(tie_count - .5, mu_count, sd_count)
win_exact <- pbinom(tie_count, n_voters, p, lower.tail = FALSE)
win_normal <- pnorm(tie_count + .5, mu_count, sd_count, lower.tail = FALSE)
data.frame(event = c("Tie", "Strict victory"),
           binomial = c(tie_exact, win_exact),
           normal_with_correction = c(tie_normal, win_normal),
           simulated = c(mean(counts == tie_count), mean(counts > tie_count)))

k <- 75:125
plot(c(75, 125), c(0, .062), type = "n",
     xlab = "Votes for A", ylab = "Mass / density per vote")
rect(k - .5, 0, k + .5, dbinom(k, n_voters, p),
     col = "#E5EDF1", border = "#A6BBC7")
curve(dnorm(x, mu_count, sd_count), add = TRUE, lwd = 3, col = "#176B87")
z <- seq(tie_count - .5, tie_count + .5, length.out = 101)
polygon(c(min(z), z, max(z)), c(0, dnorm(z, mu_count, sd_count), 0),
        col = adjustcolor("#A44A3F", .6), border = NA)

# The same tie bin expressed in percentage-point margin units:
margin_mu <- 100 * (2 * p - 1)
margin_sd <- 200 * sd_count / n_voters
tie_from_margin <- pnorm(100 / n_voters, margin_mu, margin_sd) -
                   pnorm(-100 / n_voters, margin_mu, margin_sd)
c(tie_from_count_units = tie_normal, tie_from_margin_units = tie_from_margin)
```

Each PMF bar has width one vote, so its height and area have the same
numerical value. A normal density has probability **over a bin**, not at a
point. The tie bin is 99.5 to 100.5 votes. A strict victory begins at its
upper boundary, 100.5.

The count and percentage-margin density heights have different units.
Probabilities agree after transforming both the distribution and interval.

## 6. A continuous margin gives a discrete contract payoff

Continue with the **hypothetical** forecast $\operatorname{Norm}(3,5)$.
A contract pays \$2 if the candidate wins and zero otherwise. It costs
\$1.50. Ignore fees and interest. This is a probability example, not a
description of a real market.

**Predict:** Does a probability of profit above one half guarantee positive
expected profit?

```{r}
#| label: demo-6-contract
set.seed(93006)
n_sim <- 50000
mu <- 3
sigma <- 5
prize <- 2
price <- 1.50
margins <- rnorm(n_sim, mu, sigma)
win <- margins > 0
payout <- ifelse(win, prize, 0)
profit <- payout - price
p_win <- pnorm(0, mu, sigma, lower.tail = FALSE)
pmf <- data.frame(profit = c(-price, prize - price),
                  probability = c(1 - p_win, p_win))
pmf
data.frame(
  quantity = c("Expected profit", "Profit variance", "P(positive profit)"),
  exact = c(prize * p_win - price, prize^2 * p_win * (1 - p_win), p_win),
  simulated = c(mean(profit), var(profit), mean(profit > 0))
)
c(break_even_price = prize * p_win)
```

Keep each payout tied to its corresponding margin draw. Do not independently
draw another win indicator. Subtracting a fixed price shifts all profits by
the same amount and leaves their variance unchanged.

## 7. A finite population, its PMF, and its CDF

Four potential project partners have minimum acceptable payments of 5, 15,
15, and 45 points. Randomly choose one person with equal probability.
This is a made-up teaching population, not the B2 dataset.

**Predict:** Are the three distinct minimum payments equally likely?

```{r}
#| label: demo-7-population
costs <- c(5, 15, 15, 45)
values <- sort(unique(costs))
counts <- as.numeric(table(factor(costs, levels = values)))
probability <- counts / length(costs)
cdf <- cumsum(probability)
data.frame(value = values, count = counts, probability = probability, cdf = cdf)
mu_cost <- sum(values * probability)
variance_cost <- sum((values - mu_cost)^2 * probability)
c(mean = mu_cost, population_variance = variance_cost,
  direct_variance = mean((costs - mean(costs))^2),
  R_sample_variance = var(costs))
plot(ecdf(costs), verticals = TRUE, do.points = TRUE,
     xlim = c(0, 50), col = "#176B87", lwd = 2,
     main = "CDF for the four-person population",
     xlab = "Payment threshold (points)", ylab = "Cumulative probability")
c(at_most_15 = mean(costs <= 15), below_15 = mean(costs < 15))
```

`ecdf(costs)` gives the exact CDF for a uniform draw from these four entries.
Here we define those entries as our entire population. We make no claim
about a larger population. R's `var(costs)` uses denominator $N-1$;
the finite-population variance here uses $N$.

## 8. The payoff against a mean partner and crossing CDFs

The project has an 80-point budget. Choose an offer before drawing a partner.
If the offer meets their minimum, you retain the rest of the budget;
otherwise you receive zero.

```{r}
#| label: demo-8-payoffs
set.seed(93008)
n_sim <- 50000
costs <- c(5, 15, 15, 45)
budget <- 80
earnings <- function(cost, offer) ifelse(cost <= offer, budget - offer, 0)
y15 <- earnings(costs, 15)
y45 <- earnings(costs, 45)
comparison <- data.frame(
  offer = c(15, 45),
  payoff_against_mean = c(earnings(mean(costs), 15),
                          earnings(mean(costs), 45)),
  expected_payoff = c(mean(y15), mean(y45)),
  population_variance = c(mean((y15 - mean(y15))^2),
                          mean((y45 - mean(y45))^2)),
  probability_above_20 = c(mean(y15 > 20), mean(y45 > 20)),
  probability_above_50 = c(mean(y15 > 50), mean(y45 > 50))
)
comparison
plot(ecdf(y15), xlim = c(-5, 75), ylim = c(0, 1),
     verticals = TRUE, do.points = TRUE, col = "#176B87", lwd = 2,
     main = "Two payoff CDFs", xlab = "Earnings (points)",
     ylab = "Cumulative probability")
plot(ecdf(y45), add = TRUE, verticals = TRUE, do.points = TRUE,
     col = "#A44A3F", lty = 2, lwd = 2)
legend("topleft", c("Offer 15", "Offer 45"),
       col = c("#176B87", "#A44A3F"), lty = c(1, 2), lwd = 2, bty = "n")
partners <- sample(costs, size = n_sim, replace = TRUE)
data.frame(offer = c(15, 45), exact = c(mean(y15), mean(y45)),
           simulated = c(mean(earnings(partners, 15)),
                         mean(earnings(partners, 45))))
```

Offer 15 has higher expected earnings, but offer 45 is more likely to exceed
20 points. The ordering reverses at a 50-point threshold. The mean alone
does not determine the whole distribution.

Drawing from the full four-person vector preserves the repeated value 15.
Sampling the three distinct values uniformly would change the population.

## 9. A guided function and loop over offers

This example calculates each offer's payoff for every possible partner.
There is no randomness in that calculation. Simulation appears in Demo 8.

**Before running:** Trace the loop once with an offer of 15. Identify
which objects describe an offer, a partner, a vector of payoffs, and a
table row.

```{r}
#| label: demo-9-loop
costs <- c(5, 15, 15, 45)
summarize_project <- function(costs, budget = 80) {
  result <- data.frame(offer = 0:budget, acceptance = NA_real_,
                       expected = NA_real_, variance = NA_real_)
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(result))) {
    offer <- result$offer[i]
    accepted <- costs <= offer
    payoff <- ifelse(accepted, budget - offer, 0)
    result$acceptance[i] <- mean(accepted)
    result$expected[i] <- mean(payoff)
    result$variance[i] <- mean((payoff - mean(payoff))^2)
  }
  result
}
offers <- summarize_project(costs)
offers[offers$offer %in% c(0, 5, 15, 25, 45, 80), ]
best <- abs(offers$expected - max(offers$expected)) < 1e-10
offers[best, ]
plot(offers$offer, offers$expected, type = "l",
     col = "#176B87", lwd = 2,
     xlab = "Offer (points)", ylab = "Expected earnings (points)")
```

`NA_real_` reserves numeric cells that the loop will fill. The function
returns its last expression, `result`. Row index `i` differs from the offer:
row 1 corresponds to offer 0. Store the complete table, but display only
the rows needed for interpretation.

**Try:** Give a second toy population to the same function. Which quantities
change? In B2, use the supplied data and your own derived payoff formulas.
